title: What changes when Bitcoin runs a Taproot script?
dek: A Taproot script can count signatures one at a time. Empty slots, failed checks and the cost of verification each have a precise meaning.

blocks.text: A script can require several people to approve a payment. In tapscript, it checks their signatures one at a time and counts the ones that pass. A signer who does not take part leaves an empty slot. An invalid signature stops the script.

BIP 342 defines these execution rules for Taproot. It replaces the old multisignature opcode, changes how signature checks are charged, and reserves space for future upgrades. The script still has to be the one the output committed to; BIP 341 checks that part before tapscript runs.

figure.title: Counting the signatures that arrive
figure.caption: A symbolic threshold policy: each valid signature adds one, an empty slot adds nothing, and the final count must equal the script’s requirement. OP_CHECKMULTISIG itself is disabled in tapscript.

sections.heading: From the witness to the stack

blocks.text: The witness supplies the script, its control block, and the data the script will use. After Taproot has checked the commitment, that data becomes the starting stack. Normal execution must finish with exactly one true element; OP_SUCCESS opcodes, discussed below, bypass execution entirely.

blocks.title: What reaches the interpreter
blocks.caption: The script and control block establish what may run. The remaining witness items become its inputs.

blocks.summary: Where tapscript applies and the order of validation

blocks.text: BIP 342 applies only in one situation: a version 1, 32-byte Taproot output, spent by its script path, with leaf version 0xc0. Spends with other leaf versions simply succeed under BIP 341, leaving them for future rules. The checks happen in a fixed order. First, anything BIP 141 or BIP 341 rejects is rejected. Then the script is decoded, the starting stack is checked against resource limits, the script runs, and it must finish with exactly one element on the stack, and that element must be true.
The execution rules themselves start from those of P2WSH, SegWit version 0’s script spends, and change a short list of things. The rest of this chapter walks through that list.

sections.heading: An empty slot is different from a bad signature

blocks.text: OP_CHECKSIG and OP_CHECKSIGVERIFY use 32-byte public keys to check BIP 340 Schnorr signatures. The signed message includes the Taproot transaction digest and a tapscript extension identifying the leaf, the key version and the last executed OP_CODESEPARATOR. A signature therefore authorizes this script, through its leaf hash.

A signature opcode fails if it cannot take the required items from the stack or if the public key is empty. With a 32-byte key, a non-empty signature must pass BIP 340 verification. A bad signature ends the script immediately; it does not merely contribute false.

An empty signature deliberately skips that check. OP_CHECKSIG pushes false and continues; OP_CHECKSIGVERIFY fails. A non-empty key of another length is reserved for future signature schemes: today, a non-empty signature with such a key counts as success without cryptographic verification.

blocks.title: What a signature opcode does
blocks.caption: The rules for CHECKSIG, CHECKSIGVERIFY and CHECKSIGADD, one tray per shape of key and signature. Under each tray, the recorded witnesses that land in it.

blocks.text: OP_CHECKSIGADD takes a public key, a running count n and a signature. A valid signature adds one to n; an empty signature leaves n unchanged. A threshold script can check its first key with OP_CHECKSIG, use OP_CHECKSIGADD for each remaining key, then compare the total with the required count. Each key has its own witness slot.
Try an accepted witness and its rejected counterpart below. Follow the stack until they diverge: an empty signature, an empty key and an invalid signature lead to different outcomes.

blocks.title: Recorded tapscript runs
blocks.caption: Six Core test cases, twelve recorded witnesses. Every recorded verdict matches Core’s own label, and every control block was checked against its output key first.

blocks.text: Tapscript disables OP_CHECKMULTISIG and OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY. Run one, and the script fails on the spot, exactly as OP_RETURN would; in a branch that is not taken it is ignored. The authors chose an outright failure so that anyone still writing the old opcode notices immediately.

Its replacement is OP_CHECKSIGADD. It pops a key, a number n and a signature; a valid signature pushes n + 1 and an empty one pushes n unchanged. The authors note that the old multisignature opcodes cannot be batch verified, and that the new one does the work of four existing opcodes in one byte. Their suggested rewrite of a k-of-n policy is a chain: check the first key with OP_CHECKSIG, add each further key with OP_CHECKSIGADD, and compare the total with k. Each signer’s slot in the witness holds either a signature or an empty vector.

That is not the only design. They also describe putting each k-of-k combination in its own leaf, aggregating each combination into one key, or using threshold signatures, each trading privacy, cost and interaction differently.

The explorer replays six spends from Bitcoin Core’s validation tests, each with a witness Core accepts and one it rejects. Step through them opcode by opcode. In one, a valid signature turns 23 into 24 and the script compares the result; in its failing twin, n is five bytes long, and the BIP says that MUST fail. Another hands OP_CHECKSIGADD an empty signature and pays nothing for it, while its failure script hands it an empty key instead.

The CHECKMULTISIG case shows the change most plainly. Its success witness runs a one-key OP_CHECKSIG. Its failure witness tries the same 1-of-1 policy with OP_CHECKMULTISIG, which fails the moment it executes, before any signature is looked at.

sections.heading: The witness pays for its checks

blocks.text: Older scripts count signature operations against a limit for the whole block. Tapscript signature operations are left out of that count. Instead each input gets its own budget: 50 plus the size of its witness in bytes. Every signature opcode run with a non-empty signature subtracts 50, and if the budget drops below zero the script fails. The authors’ reason is practical: a second block-wide limit, alongside weight, made it harder to choose transactions for a block.

A normal signature brings enough bytes to pay for its own check. With a 32-byte key, it is 64 or 65 bytes long, plus a length prefix; its check costs 50. An empty signature costs nothing. Unknown key types still incur the charge for a non-empty signature, even though they skip verification.

blocks.title: A signature pays its own way
blocks.caption: A checked signature brings its own bytes and a length byte into the witness, and so into the budget; its check costs less than that. An empty signature costs nothing.

blocks.text: Other limits move too. The 10,000-byte script size limit and the 201 non-push opcode limit do not apply to tapscript. The limit of 1,000 stack elements remains and now also covers the starting stack taken from the witness, and elements still may not exceed 520 bytes.

sections.heading: Rules left for a future upgrade

blocks.text: OP_SUCCESSx opcodes leave room for future soft forks. After the BIP 141 and BIP 341 checks, encountering one while decoding makes the spend valid immediately. The interpreter does not run the script, and even undecodable bytes after that opcode do not change the result. The recorded example uses OP_SUCCESS126. The BIP warns that using an undefined OP_SUCCESS opcode is insecure and can lose funds.

blocks.title: A trapdoor in the decoder
blocks.caption: Core case 50’s two witnesses. An OP_SUCCESS opcode ends validation, valid, before anything runs; OP_NOP runs and leaves an empty stack.

blocks.text: One rule went the other way, from advice to consensus. In P2WSH, MINIMALIF is only a standardness rule; in tapscript, OP_IF and OP_NOTIF must receive exactly an empty vector or the single byte 0x01. In the recorded MINIMALIF case, the failing witness offers a three-byte value instead, and the script stops at OP_IF.

blocks.title: OP_IF takes 0x01 or the empty vector
blocks.caption: Core case 662: the success witness gives OP_IF the byte 0x01; the failure witness gives it a longer value, and the script stops there.

blocks.label: Caveat
blocks.text: The figure is a player for recorded runs, not a script interpreter. The recorder behind it supports a small reviewed set of opcodes and refuses anything else, so it cannot quietly accept a script it does not understand. A trace reaching true here says nothing about scripts outside these six cases.

blocks.summary: Sources and the limits of these recordings

blocks.text: BIP 342 was assigned in 2020 and deployed with BIP 341. Its authors changed the language alongside Taproot because Schnorr signatures, batch validation and the new signature hash required different opcode behavior.

BIP 342 says that BIP 341’s test vectors contain tapscript examples. The wallet vector file pinned for this site contains tapscript leaves but no script path spends, so there is nothing there to execute. BIP 341 also links Bitcoin Core’s validation test vectors, on the main branch of Core’s test-asset repository; this site chose one commit of that file, and this chapter uses six cases from it, copied and checked by hash.

Two of the cases are upgrade hooks: an OP_SUCCESS opcode and an unknown key type. Core’s tests show what consensus accepts, not what is safe; the BIP warns against using OP_SUCCESS opcodes before a soft fork defines them, and unknown key types exist only so that one can.

Each recorded run was checked twice at build time: the control block against the output key, as in the previous chapter, and the final verdict against Core’s label. If either check had disagreed, this page would not have been built.
